overview: The Deeds Office (under the Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development) is responsible for registering ownership of property in South Africa. Every property transfer, bond registration, and servitude must be registered here. The Durban Deeds Office serves the KwaZulu-Natal region. The Deeds Registry is a public record — anyone can search it to verify ownership, bonds, and conditions on a property.

services.name: Title Deed Search
services.description: Check who owns a specific property, what bonds are registered against it, and if there are any restrictions (servitudes, conditions, endorsements).
how: Visit the Durban Deeds Office in person — searches are done at the public search counter (morning only, 08:00-12:00, bring your ID)
You can search by property description (erf number + township name) or by owner name
A basic search costs approximately R30 per property
You can also use the online DeedsWeb portal (www.deedsweb.gov.za) — registration required, R30 per search
For more detailed information, engage a conveyancing attorney
search_results_include: Registered owner name and ID number
Property description (erf number, township, extent in square metres)
Registered mortgage bonds (which bank, bond amount)
Servitudes (rights of way, municipal access, Eskom power lines)
Conditions of title (building restrictions, use restrictions)
why_you_might_need_this: Buying property — confirm the seller is the registered owner before paying any money
Boundary disputes — confirm exact property descriptions and compare to Surveyor-General diagrams
Debt collection — check if a debtor owns property
Estate administration — identify deceased person's property
Verifying legitimacy — protect yourself from property scams

services.name: Property Transfer
services.description: When property changes hands (sale, donation, inheritance), the transfer must be registered at the Deeds Office. Only a registered conveyancer (not just any attorney) can handle property transfers.
process: A registered conveyancing attorney handles the transfer — this is legally required (verify the conveyancer's registration with the Legal Practice Council)
The attorney prepares all transfer documents including the deed of transfer
Both buyer and seller sign documents at the attorney's office
Transfer duty must be paid to SARS before lodgement (the attorney handles this)
A rates clearance certificate must be obtained from the municipality
The attorney lodges documents at the Deeds Office
The Deeds Office examines and registers the transfer — processing time approximately 2-3 weeks after lodgement
The new title deed is issued in the buyer's name
costs: Transfer duty: payable to SARS — see transfer_duty_table below
Conveyancing fees: see conveyancing_fees_guideline below — shop around, these are guidelines not fixed prices
Deeds Office fees: approximately R700-R2,000 depending on the transaction
Rates clearance certificate from the municipality: R100-R500 depending on the municipality
FICA compliance costs (certified ID copies, proof of address)

services.name: Bond Registration
services.description: When you take a home loan, the bank registers a mortgage bond against your property at the Deeds Office. The bond gives the bank the right to sell the property if you default on the loan.
process: Your bank appoints a bond attorney (the bank chooses, not you — but you pay the fees)
The attorney prepares bond documents
You sign at the attorney's office
The attorney lodges at the Deeds Office
Registration takes approximately 2-3 weeks
The bond is noted against your title deed in the Deeds Office records

services.name: Bond Cancellation
services.description: When you pay off your home loan in full, the bond must be cancelled at the Deeds Office. The bank is obligated to cancel the bond — do not let them delay.
process: Notify your bank that the loan is paid in full
The bank instructs a cancellation attorney
The attorney prepares cancellation documents and lodges at the Deeds Office
The bank should cover the cancellation attorney's fees — do not pay this yourself
Cancellation takes approximately 2-3 weeks after lodgement
Confirm the bond has been cancelled by checking at the Deeds Office or on DeedsWeb

transfer_duty_table.description: Transfer duty is a tax paid to SARS when property is acquired. The rates below apply to natural persons (individuals). Companies and trusts pay a flat 12% on the full value. Transfer duty must be paid before the Deeds Office will register the transfer.
transfer_duty_table.effective_date: As per current SARS schedule — always confirm with SARS or your conveyancer as rates may change in the annual Budget Speech

brackets.example: Property worth R900,000 = R0 transfer duty
Property worth R1,400,000 = 3% x R300,000 = R9,000

brackets.rate: R12,375 + 6% of the value above R1,512,500
R48,675 + 8% of the value above R2,117,500
R97,075 + 11% of the value above R2,722,500
R1,128,600 + 13% of the value above R12,100,000

important_notes: First-time buyers still pay transfer duty — there is no exemption, only the 0% bracket up to R1.1M helps
Transfer duty is based on the purchase price or market value, whichever is higher
VAT-registered sellers charge VAT instead of transfer duty — you do not pay both
Transfer duty must be paid within 6 months of the transaction date
The conveyancing attorney usually handles the SARS transfer duty submission on your behalf

conveyancing_fees_guideline.description: Conveyancing fees are what the attorney charges to handle the property transfer. These are guideline tariffs — not fixed by law. You can and should shop around for competitive quotes. Always use a registered conveyancer (not just any attorney). Verify registration with the Legal Practice Council or Law Society of South Africa.

guideline_fees.note: Includes attorney fee, Deeds Office fee, and postage/petties
Includes attorney fee, Deeds Office fee, and postage/petties
Includes attorney fee, Deeds Office fee, and postage/petties
At higher values, fees become more negotiable — always get multiple quotes

what_the_fee_covers: Obtaining rates clearance certificate from municipality
Liaison with buyer, seller, banks, and other attorneys
Attending to any Deeds Office queries or rejections
tips: Get at least 3 quotes before choosing a conveyancer
Ask for a detailed breakdown — not just a lump sum
Verify the conveyancer is registered with the Legal Practice Council (www.lpc.org.za)
The seller usually appoints the transferring attorney in a sale, but you can negotiate this
Bond registration attorney is appointed by the bank — you cannot choose, but you pay the fees

deedsweb_portal.description: DeedsWeb is the official online portal for searching the Deeds Registry from anywhere. You do not need to visit the Deeds Office in person if you use DeedsWeb.
how_to_register: Click on 'Register' to create a new account
Complete the registration form with your personal details and valid email
You will receive a confirmation email — follow the link to activate your account
Once activated, you can top up your account with credit to perform searches
search_options: Search by property description: you need the erf number and township name (e.g., Erf 1234 Umbilo)
Search by owner name: enter the registered owner's name to find all properties registered to them
Search by ID number: find all properties registered to a specific person
results_include: Registered owner name and identity number
Full property description (erf number, township, extent)
All registered mortgage bonds (bank, bond amount, date of registration)
tips: You need the correct erf number and township name — get this from your rates account or the municipality
If you are searching by owner name, try variations (initials vs full names)
DeedsWeb is available 24/7 but may have maintenance downtime
Print or save your search results — you are charged per search, not per page view

property_alert.description: Property Alert is a free early-warning service from the Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development. It notifies you by SMS or email if any transaction (transfer, bond, cancellation) is lodged against your property at the Deeds Office. This is your best protection against property fraud.
how_to_register: SMS the word 'ALERT' to 35991 (standard SMS rates apply)
Or visit the Deeds Office in person and ask to register for Property Alert
You will need your property description (erf number and township) and your ID number
what_it_does: Sends you an SMS or email notification whenever any transaction is lodged against your registered property
This includes transfers, bond registrations, bond cancellations, and endorsements
Gives you early warning so you can take action if the transaction is fraudulent
Notifications are sent within 24 hours of lodgement at the Deeds Office
property_alert.cost: Free — there is no charge for this service
property_alert.important: Every property owner should register for Property Alert. It is the single most effective way to detect fraudulent activity on your property. If you receive a notification for a transaction you did not authorise, contact the Deeds Office and SAPS immediately.

title_deed_explained.description: A title deed is the official document that proves you own a specific property. It is registered at the Deeds Office and is the definitive proof of ownership in South Africa.
what_is_on_it: Property description: the erf number, township name, extent (size in square metres), and province
Owner details: full name, identity number, and marital status of the registered owner
How the property was acquired: whether by sale, donation, inheritance, or court order
Conditions of title: restrictions on what you can do with the property (e.g., residential use only, no subdivision without consent)
Servitudes: rights that other parties have over your property (e.g., right of way, municipal pipeline, Eskom power line)
Reference to the Surveyor-General diagram: the official survey diagram showing the exact boundaries
why_it_matters: It is your legal proof of ownership — without it, you cannot prove the property is yours
Banks require sight of the title deed before granting a home loan
The municipality uses it to confirm ownership for rates and services
In disputes (boundary, inheritance, divorce), the title deed is the primary evidence
You need it to sell, donate, or mortgage your property
It is used to verify that the person selling you a property is actually the owner
tips: Keep your original title deed in a safe place — a bank safe deposit box is ideal
If your bank holds a bond over your property, the bank keeps the title deed until the bond is cancelled
You can request a certified copy from the Deeds Office if the original is lost (see lost_title_deed section)
Always read the conditions and servitudes on your title deed — they affect what you can do with the property

sectional_title.description: Sectional title is a form of property ownership different from freehold. It applies to apartments, townhouses, and complexes where multiple owners share common property. It is governed by the Sectional Titles Act 95 of 1986 and the Sectional Titles Schemes Management Act 8 of 2011.
how_it_differs_from_freehold: You own your individual unit (called a 'section') but share ownership of common property (gardens, parking, driveways, pools) with all other owners
A Body Corporate is established to manage the common property and enforce rules
You must pay monthly levies to the Body Corporate for maintenance, insurance, and administration
You are bound by conduct rules and management rules — you cannot do whatever you want
Building alterations require Body Corporate approval (even inside your unit in some cases)
The Body Corporate has the right to levy special contributions for unexpected expenses (e.g., roof repair)
levies: Levies are mandatory monthly payments to the Body Corporate
They cover insurance of the building, maintenance of common areas, security, water, refuse, and administration
Levy amounts vary — typically R800-R5,000+ per month depending on the complex
If you do not pay your levies, the Body Corporate can get a court order and attach your property
Levy arrears transfer to the new owner on sale — always check levy clearance before buying
transfer_differences: The conveyancer needs a Body Corporate consent letter before lodging the transfer
A levy clearance certificate must be obtained from the managing agent — this confirms all levies are paid up to date
A compliance certificate under the Community Schemes Ombud Service Act may be required
The buyer must be given a copy of the conduct rules and management rules before transfer
Transfer may take longer because of the extra requirements

body_corporate.what_it_is: The Body Corporate is the collective of all sectional title owners in a scheme. It is automatically created when the scheme is registered.
responsibilities: Maintains and insures the common property
Enforces conduct rules and management rules
Holds an Annual General Meeting (AGM) — all owners should attend and vote
Appoints a managing agent (optional but common) to handle day-to-day administration
your_rights_as_an_owner: You can attend and vote at AGMs
You can inspect the Body Corporate's financial records
You can challenge unreasonable rules or levies through the Community Schemes Ombud Service (CSOS)

estate_property.description: When a property owner dies, the property forms part of their deceased estate. It cannot simply be sold or transferred — it must go through a formal estate administration process overseen by the Master of the High Court.
process: Step 1: Report the death to the Master of the High Court within 14 days. Submit the death certificate, will (if any), and asset inventory
Step 2: The Master appoints an executor — either the person nominated in the will or a professional (usually an attorney or trust company)
Step 3: The executor advertises for creditors in the Government Gazette and a local newspaper (creditors have 30 days to submit claims)
Step 4: The executor prepares a Liquidation and Distribution Account showing all assets, debts, and how the estate will be distributed
Step 5: The L&D Account is advertised for inspection — anyone can object within 21 days
Step 6: Once approved, the executor distributes the estate according to the will or the Intestate Succession Act (if there is no will)

Step 7: For property — the executor either endorses the title deed to the heir (Section 42 endorsement — no transfer duty, faster) or does a formal transfer through a conveyancer (transfer duty may apply)

section_42_endorsement_vs_formal_transfe.section_42: A Section 42 endorsement is a simpler, cheaper process where the executor endorses the existing title deed in favour of the heir. No conveyancer is needed, and no transfer duty is payable. This is used when the heir inherits the property and keeps it.
section_42_endorsement_vs_formal_transfe.formal_transfer: A formal transfer is required when the property is sold from the estate to a third party, or when the estate has debts and the property must be sold to pay them. Transfer duty applies, and a conveyancer must handle the transfer.

estate_property.timeline: Estate administration typically takes 6 to 24 months, depending on complexity. Delays are common if there are disputes among heirs, missing documents, or if the Master's Office has a backlog.

masters_office_durban.what_to_bring: Death certificate, original will (if any), ID of the deceased, IDs of heirs, marriage certificate, inventory of assets and liabilities

common_issues: No will — the property is distributed according to the Intestate Succession Act, which may not match the deceased's wishes
Multiple heirs disagree on what to do with the property — the executor may need to sell and divide the proceeds
The property has an outstanding bond — the estate must continue payments or the bank may foreclose
The Master's Office is slow — follow up regularly, keep records of all submissions and reference numbers
Illegal occupation — sometimes family members or tenants refuse to vacate after the owner dies. The executor has the authority to deal with this

servitudes.description: A servitude is a right that someone else has over your property. It is registered on the title deed and runs with the land — it does not disappear when the property is sold. Servitudes can significantly affect what you can do with your property and its value.

types.description: Allows a neighbour or the public to cross your property to access their own property or a public road. Common in rural and semi-rural areas.
Allows the municipality to install, maintain, and access water pipes, sewer lines, or stormwater drains on your property. Very common in urban areas.
Allows Eskom to run power lines over or through your property and to access the property for maintenance. You cannot build under or near these power lines.
Gives a specific person the right to use your property (or its fruits/income) for their lifetime. Common in wills — e.g., 'my wife may live in the house for her lifetime'.
Restricts development to protect the environment, wetlands, or heritage sites.

how_they_affect_property_value: A servitude can reduce property value because it limits what you can build or do on that portion of land
You cannot build on a servitude area without the consent of the servitude holder (e.g., the municipality, Eskom, or the neighbour)
Insurance may be affected — some insurers exclude damage related to servitude areas
A servitude can also benefit your property — e.g., a right of way over a neighbour's land to access a main road
important_notes: Always check the title deed for servitudes before buying property
If you build on a servitude area without consent, you may be ordered to demolish at your own cost
Servitudes are registered at the Deeds Office and appear on the title deed
To cancel or amend a servitude, you generally need the consent of the servitude holder and a formal Deeds Office process
The Surveyor-General diagram shows exactly where servitudes fall on the property

boundary_disputes.description: Boundary disputes arise when neighbours disagree about where one property ends and another begins. This is more common than people think, especially with older properties, informal fencing, or where improvements encroach on neighbouring land.
how_to_resolve: Step 1: Get the Surveyor-General diagram for both properties. This is the official survey diagram showing the exact boundaries. You can get it from the Deeds Office or the Surveyor-General's office.
Step 2: Compare the Surveyor-General diagram to the title deed and to what is physically on the ground (fences, walls, beacons).
Step 3: If the diagrams are unclear or the beacons are missing, hire a professional land surveyor to re-peg the boundaries. Cost: approximately R5,000-R15,000 depending on the property.
Step 4: Try to mediate with your neighbour — show them the diagrams and surveyor's report. Many disputes can be resolved amicably.
Step 5: If mediation fails, you can approach a community advice office or the municipality's dispute resolution office.
Step 6: As a last resort, apply to the Magistrate's Court or High Court for a declaratory order confirming the boundary. You will need the surveyor's report and title deeds as evidence.
important_notes: Do not move, remove, or damage boundary beacons — this is a criminal offence under the Land Survey Act
Long-term occupation of a neighbour's land does not give you ownership (South Africa does not recognise 'squatter's rights' or adverse possession on registered land)
If a neighbour's building encroaches on your property, you may be entitled to have it removed or to claim compensation
Always try to resolve amicably before going to court — court is expensive and slow

surveyor_general_kzn.address: Durban — contact via the Deeds Office or the Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development
surveyor_general_kzn.note: The Surveyor-General's diagrams are definitive — they override fences, walls, and informal boundaries

lost_title_deed.description: If your title deed is lost, stolen, or destroyed, you can obtain a certified copy from the Deeds Office. The original title deed will be endorsed as 'lost' in the Deeds Office records.
process: Step 1: Go to your nearest SAPS station and make an affidavit (sworn statement) confirming that the title deed is lost or destroyed. Explain the circumstances (lost in a fire, stolen, misplaced, etc.)
Step 2: Take the affidavit to the Deeds Office (or have your conveyancer do it) and apply for a certified copy of the title deed
Step 3: Pay the application fee — approximately R150
Step 4: The Deeds Office will process your application — this takes approximately 2 to 4 weeks
Step 5: The original title deed is endorsed as 'lost' in the records, so it cannot be used fraudulently
Step 6: Collect your certified copy from the Deeds Office — it has the same legal standing as the original
what_you_need: Property description (erf number and township name — get this from your rates account if you do not know it)
tips: Register for Property Alert immediately if your title deed is lost or stolen — this protects against fraudulent transfers
If the title deed was held by a bank (because of a home loan bond), contact the bank — they may have it or can confirm its status
A certified copy is legally equivalent to the original — you can use it for any purpose

verification_of_ownership.description: Before buying property, you must verify that the seller is the registered owner. Property fraud is a real and growing problem in South Africa — scammers sell properties they do not own using fake title deeds and forged identity documents.
how_to_verify: Search the Deeds Office records (in person or via DeedsWeb at www.deedsweb.gov.za) to confirm the registered owner
Compare the seller's name and ID number to the registered owner on the Deeds Office records
Ask to see the original title deed — not a copy — and compare it to the Deeds Office records
If the seller claims to act on behalf of the owner (e.g., power of attorney), verify the power of attorney is genuine and has not been revoked
Use a reputable, registered conveyancer to handle the transaction — they are required to do FICA checks on both parties
red_flags: Seller is in a hurry and pressures you to pay quickly — legitimate sellers allow time for due diligence
Seller wants cash payment or payment into a personal account — always pay into the conveyancer's trust account
The title deed looks altered, has inconsistent fonts, or lacks the Deeds Office stamp
Seller cannot produce the original title deed or rates account
Property price is significantly below market value — if it seems too good to be true, it probably is
Seller's ID does not match the registered owner's details at the Deeds Office
what_to_do_if_you_suspect_fraud: Contact the Deeds Office to flag the property
Report to the Legal Practice Council if a fake attorney is involved
Register for Property Alert on the property in question

rates_clearance_certificate.description: A rates clearance certificate is a document from the municipality confirming that all municipal rates, taxes, and service charges on a property are paid up to date. It is a legal requirement for property transfer — the Deeds Office will not register a transfer without it.
process: Step 1: The conveyancing attorney applies to the municipality for the rates clearance certificate
Step 2: The municipality checks if all rates, water, electricity, sewerage, and refuse charges are paid
Step 3: If there are outstanding amounts, they must be paid before the certificate is issued — the attorney usually arranges payment from the sale proceeds
Step 4: The municipality issues the certificate — this takes 5 to 10 business days (sometimes longer with eThekwini Municipality)
Step 5: The certificate is valid for 60 days from date of issue — if the transfer is not registered within 60 days, a new certificate must be obtained
rates_clearance_certificate.cost: Approximately R100 to R500 depending on the municipality. eThekwini Municipality charges approximately R300.
important_notes: The seller is responsible for paying outstanding rates before transfer — not the buyer
If the municipality is slow in issuing the certificate, this can delay the entire transfer
The conveyancer may require the seller to pay rates in advance (up to the expected transfer date) to avoid delays
eThekwini Municipality rates clearance: apply at Customer Service Centres or via the eThekwini website

ethekwini_municipality.customer_service_centres: Multiple locations — Florence Mkhize Building (251 Anton Lembede Street, Durban CBD) is the main centre

deeds_office_durban.address: 209 Peter Mokaba Road (formerly Ridge Road), Morningside, Durban 4001
deeds_office_durban.public_search_hours: Monday to Friday 08:00-12:00 (morning only — arrive early, it gets busy)
what_to_bring: Your ID document (original — not a copy)
Property details if doing a search (erf number, township name)
Cash or card for search fees (R30 per property search)
Reference numbers for any pending applications
tips: Arrive before 08:00 for public searches — the counter closes at 12:00 and queues can be long
If you are not comfortable searching yourself, bring a conveyancer or paralegal
Parking is available on-site but limited — consider using a ride service
The staff can be helpful but are often very busy — be patient and have all your information ready

community_schemes_ombud_service.purpose: Sectional title and body corporate disputes

ethekwini_municipality.purpose: Rates clearance, rates enquiries, property valuations

common_problems.what_to_do: Make an affidavit at SAPS confirming the loss. Take the affidavit to the Deeds Office and apply for a certified copy. Cost approximately R150. Takes 2-4 weeks. The original is endorsed as 'lost' to prevent fraud. Register for Property Alert immediately.

common_problems.problem: Property registered in deceased person's name
common_problems.what_to_do: Report the death to the Master of the High Court within 14 days. The Master will appoint an executor to administer the estate. The executor will either do a Section 42 endorsement (simpler, no transfer duty) or a formal transfer. Timeline: 6-24 months. Master's Office Durban: 031 372 3000, 2 Devonshire Place.

common_problems.problem: Property sold but transfer not registered
common_problems.what_to_do: Contact the conveyancing attorney who handled the sale — demand a status update in writing. If the attorney is unresponsive or has absconded, lodge a complaint with the Legal Practice Council: 012 366 8800 or www.lpc.org.za. You may have a claim against the Attorneys Fidelity Fund.

common_problems.problem: Suspicious activity on your title deed (someone trying to transfer without your knowledge)
common_problems.what_to_do: If you receive a Property Alert notification for a transaction you did not authorise: (1) Contact the Deeds Office immediately to flag the property, (2) Open a case at SAPS — this is fraud, (3) Contact the Legal Practice Council if a conveyancer is involved, (4) Apply for an urgent court interdict to prevent the transfer if it has not yet been registered.

The seller must pay all outstanding rates, water, and service charges before the municipality will issue a rates clearance certificate. The conveyancer can arrange for payment from the sale proceeds. Contact eThekwini Municipality: 031 311 1111.

common_problems.problem: Body Corporate not issuing consent or levy clearance for sectional title transfer
common_problems.what_to_do: The managing agent must issue a levy clearance certificate. If the Body Corporate is obstructive, contact the Community Schemes Ombud Service (CSOS) at 010 593 0533 or www.csos.org.za. They can intervene and order compliance.

Get the Surveyor-General diagram from the Deeds Office. Hire a land surveyor to re-peg the boundaries if beacons are missing (cost R5,000-R15,000). Try to mediate with the neighbour. If that fails, apply for a declaratory order from the Magistrate's Court or High Court.

You should not have built on the servitude area without the consent of the servitude holder (municipality, Eskom, neighbour). The servitude holder can demand demolition at your cost. Try to negotiate — you may be able to get retrospective consent or relocate the servitude. Consult a property attorney.

Do not pay any money. Verify ownership at the Deeds Office or via DeedsWeb (www.deedsweb.gov.za). Compare the seller's ID to the registered owner. Report to SAPS immediately. Contact the Deeds Office to flag the property. If a fake attorney is involved, report to the Legal Practice Council.

common_scams.description: Property fraud is a serious and growing problem in South Africa. Be vigilant and always verify before paying.

types.how_it_works: Scammers create forged title deeds and sell property they do not own. The fake deed may look authentic but will not match Deeds Office records.
types.how_to_protect_yourself: Always verify ownership at the Deeds Office or via DeedsWeb before paying any money. Use a registered conveyancer who will do proper checks.

types.how_it_works: Fraudsters use forged identity documents or powers of attorney to instruct a conveyancer to transfer property without the real owner knowing. This often targets elderly people, absentee owners, or deceased estates.
types.how_to_protect_yourself: Register for Property Alert (SMS 'ALERT' to 35991) — you will be notified of any transaction lodged against your property. Act immediately if you receive an unexpected notification.

types.how_it_works: Someone poses as a conveyancer or attorney, collects money into a personal account, and disappears. They may have a professional-looking office and website.
types.how_to_protect_yourself: Verify the conveyancer's registration with the Legal Practice Council (www.lpc.org.za or 012 366 8800). Never pay into a personal account — only pay into the conveyancer's trust account. Check that the trust account is registered.

types.how_it_works: Scammers list properties for sale or rent that they do not own, often at below-market prices to attract victims. They collect deposits and disappear.
types.how_to_protect_yourself: Verify ownership at the Deeds Office. Visit the property in person. Use reputable estate agents registered with the Property Practitioners Regulatory Authority (PPRA). Never pay a deposit without a written agreement and verification.

types.how_it_works: Scammers intercept emails between the conveyancer and buyer, and send fake banking details. The buyer pays into the scammer's account instead of the attorney's trust account.
types.how_to_protect_yourself: Always confirm banking details telephonically with the conveyancer using a number you verified independently (not from the email). Never change payment details based on an email alone.

escalation.step_1: Contact the Durban Deeds Office directly: 031 309 2950
escalation.step_2: Escalate to the Chief Registrar of Deeds in Pretoria: 012 338 7200
escalation.step_3: Lodge a complaint with the Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development
escalation.step_4: If a conveyancer or attorney is involved in wrongdoing, report to the Legal Practice Council: 012 366 8800 or www.lpc.org.za
escalation.step_5: For sectional title disputes, contact the Community Schemes Ombud Service (CSOS): 010 593 0533
escalation.step_6: For municipal delays (rates clearance), escalate to the eThekwini Municipal Ombudsman or your ward councillor
escalation.step_7: For fraud, open a case at SAPS and consider applying for an urgent court interdict
legislation: Sectional Titles Schemes Management Act 8 of 2011
Community Schemes Ombud Service Act 9 of 2011

your_rights: Section 25 of the Constitution protects property rights — no one may be deprived of property except in terms of a law of general application
You have the right to search the Deeds Office records — they are public records, anyone can search them
You have the right to a certified copy of your title deed if the original is lost
The Property Alert service is free and helps protect against fraudulent transfers
You have the right to choose your own conveyancer for a transfer (but the bank chooses the bond attorney)
You have the right to inspect Body Corporate financial records if you are a sectional title owner
You have the right to challenge municipal property valuations through the objection process
You have the right to report attorney or conveyancer misconduct to the Legal Practice Council
You have the right to approach the Community Schemes Ombud Service for sectional title disputes
